whyNext: Builds on tree depth-first exploration from Binary Tree Inorder Traversal (Seq 139) by recording node values in left-right-root order both recursively and iteratively.
hints: In postorder traversal, a node is processed only after both its left and right subtrees have been completely visited.
Recursive traversal visits root.left, then root.right, then adds root.val.
Iterative approach: do a modified preorder (root -> right -> left) and reverse the collected list, or use a stack with a prev pointer to detect returning from the right child.

brute.idea: Standard recursive postorder traversal: recurse on left child, recurse on right child, then record root value.
steps: Create an empty result list.
Define postorder(node): if node == null return; postorder(node.left); postorder(node.right); list.add(node.val).
Call postorder(root) and return list.
brute.whySlow: Recursive call stack relies on system memory which can overflow for deep trees.

optimal.idea: Iterative traversal using a stack: push root, traverse root -> right -> left, and prepend each node value to a LinkedList (or reverse at the end).
steps: If root is null, return empty list.
Initialize stack and push root.
While stack is not empty: pop node, add node.val to head of linked list.
Push node.left, then push node.right.
Return list.

whyNext: Builds on BFS level grouping from Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (Seq 135) by summing node values per level using 64-bit integers and computing the floating-point level average.
hints: Use BFS with a queue. In each level iteration, queue.size() gives the exact count of nodes in the current tree level.
Sum values using a double or long to prevent 32-bit integer overflow.
For each level: double sum = 0; int size = queue.size(); repeat size times: node = queue.poll(); sum += node.val; enqueue children. Add sum / size to result list.

brute.idea: Collect all node values level by level into a list of lists using DFS, then calculate average of each level list.
steps: Use DFS with level index to store values in List<List<Integer>>.
For each level list, compute average of elements.
Collect averages and return.
brute.whySlow: Requires storing all tree node values explicitly in lists before computing averages.

optimal.idea: Queue-based BFS: sum values directly on the fly level by level using O(width) auxiliary space.
steps: If root is null, return empty list.
Initialize Queue<TreeNode> and add root.
While queue is not empty: int sz = queue.size(), double sum = 0.
Loop sz times: poll node, sum += node.val, enqueue non-null left and right children.
Add sum / sz to result list. Return result list.

whyNext: Inverts the result ordering from Average of Levels in Binary Tree (Seq 396) by collecting level node lists and reversing them into bottom-up level order.
hints: Traverse top-down using standard BFS level order traversal.
Store each level's node values in a list.
Prepend each level to the front of a LinkedList, or reverse the top-down result list before returning.

brute.idea: Standard BFS level order traversal followed by Collections.reverse.
steps: Collect top-down level lists using standard BFS.
Reverse the full list of levels.
Return reversed list.
brute.whySlow: Requires post-processing reversal step on the entire outer list.

optimal.idea: Prepend each level directly to a LinkedList in O(1) time per level without requiring full array reversal.
steps: Use LinkedList<List<Integer>> res.
BFS with queue: at each level, extract all nodes of that level into a list.
Call res.addFirst(level).
Return res.

whyNext: Adapts level-wise reduction from Average of Levels in Binary Tree (Seq 396) by tracking the maximum node value instead of the sum at each BFS level.
hints: Use BFS level order traversal.
Initialize maxVal = Integer.MIN_VALUE at the start of each level.
Iterate through all nodes in the current level, updating maxVal = Math.max(maxVal, node.val), and add maxVal to the result list.

brute.idea: DFS traversal collecting all values level by level in a Map<Integer, List<Integer>>, then finding the maximum of each level.
steps: Traverse tree with DFS tracking level depth.
Collect node values in Map<Integer, List<Integer>>.
For each level in map, find maximum value.
Collect maximums in order and return.
brute.whySlow: Requires storing all tree nodes in lists before finding max values.

optimal.idea: BFS level-order traversal updating maximum value in O(1) space per level.
steps: If root is null, return empty list.
Initialize queue with root.
While queue is not empty: sz = queue.size(), maxVal = Integer.MIN_VALUE.
Loop sz times: pop node, maxVal = Math.max(maxVal, node.val), enqueue non-null children.
Add maxVal to result list. Return result list.

whyNext: Builds on BFS level row scanning from Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row (Seq 398) by visiting right child before left child so the final polled node in the queue is guaranteed to be the bottom-left value.
hints: Standard BFS processes left child then right child, so the first node polled in each level is the leftmost.
Clever BFS variation: enqueue right child first, then left child. Then the very last node polled in the entire BFS traversal is the bottom-left node.
Initialize queue with root. While !q.isEmpty(): node = q.poll(); if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right); if (node.left != null) q.offer(node.left). Return node.val.

brute.idea: DFS keeping track of maximum depth seen and recording the first node encountered at any new depth.
steps: Maintain maxDepth = -1 and leftmostVal.
DFS(node, depth): if node == null return.
If depth > maxDepth, update maxDepth = depth and leftmostVal = node.val.
Recurse left child with depth + 1, then right child with depth + 1.
Return leftmostVal.
brute.whySlow: Requires recursive stack and depth comparisons across all nodes.

optimal.idea: Right-to-left BFS: enqueue right child then left child so the last node popped from the queue is the bottom-left node.
steps: Initialize queue with root.
While queue is not empty: pop node.
If node.right is not null, push node.right.
If node.left is not null, push node.left.
When queue becomes empty, return last popped node's value.

whyNext: Builds on recursive tree reconstruction from Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (Seq 124) by summing overlapping node values and recursing on both left and right subtrees simultaneously.
hints: If one of the two nodes is null, the merged tree takes the other node entirely.
If both nodes are non-null, create a new node (or reuse root1) whose value is root1.val + root2.val.
Recurse: merged.left = mergeTrees(root1.left, root2.left) and merged.right = mergeTrees(root1.right, root2.right). Return merged.

brute.idea: Explicitly allocate a brand new TreeNode for every merged position using simultaneous BFS.
steps: If root1 == null return root2; if root2 == null return root1.
Use queues to hold pairs of corresponding nodes from both trees.
Create new TreeNode with sum of values.
Merge left children and right children accordingly.
Return root of merged tree.
brute.whySlow: Allocating auxiliary pairs and queue elements creates unnecessary heap allocation overhead.

optimal.idea: Recursive in-place merging: reuse root1 node, add root2.val to root1.val, and recurse on left and right children.
steps: If root1 == null return root2.
If root2 == null return root1.
root1.val += root2.val.
root1.left = mergeTrees(root1.left, root2.left).
root1.right = mergeTrees(root1.right, root2.right).
Return root1.

whyNext: Builds on root-to-leaf path tracking from Path Sum (Seq 131) by accumulating decimal path values (current * 10 + node.val) and summing them across all leaf nodes.
hints: Every step down the tree multiplies the accumulated parent value by 10 and adds the current node's value.
A leaf node has both left and right children as null.
In dfs(node, cur): if node == null return 0. Compute cur = cur * 10 + node.val. If node is leaf return cur. Return dfs(node.left, cur) + dfs(node.right, cur).

brute.idea: Traverse all paths from root to leaf, store the path strings in a list, parse each string into an integer, and sum them.
steps: Use DFS to find all root-to-leaf path strings.
Store strings in an ArrayList.
Parse each string into an integer and sum up all values.
Return the total sum.
brute.whySlow: String construction and conversions add extra memory allocations and overhead.

optimal.idea: Direct integer accumulation DFS: carry current path value as an integer argument, summing leaf values directly in O(h) space.
steps: Define dfs(node, currentSum).
If node is null, return 0.
currentSum = currentSum * 10 + node.val.
If node is a leaf (left and right are null), return currentSum.
Return dfs(node.left, currentSum) + dfs(node.right, currentSum).

whyNext: Builds on ancestor relationship tracking from Lowest Common Ancestor (Seq 133) by passing the running minimum and maximum values along each path from root to leaf to maximize abs(ancestor - descendant).
hints: Any node's maximum difference with its ancestors on a path is determined by the minimum and maximum ancestor values along that path.
Pass minVal and maxVal down from root in DFS.
At each node: update minVal = min(minVal, node.val) and maxVal = max(maxVal, node.val). At a leaf, the max difference for this branch is maxVal - minVal.

brute.idea: For every node, traverse all descendant nodes in its subtree to compute the maximum difference abs(root.val - descendant.val).
steps: Traverse tree; for each node u, run a helper DFS exploring all nodes in u's subtree.
Compute abs(u.val - v.val) for every descendant v.
Update the global maximum difference found.
brute.whySlow: Visiting subtrees repeatedly results in O(n^2) time for degenerate trees.

optimal.idea: Top-down min/max tracking: pass minimum and maximum seen so far down each path; at leaves return max - min.
steps: In dfs(node, curMin, curMax): if node == null return curMax - curMin.
Update curMin = Math.min(curMin, node.val).
Update curMax = Math.max(curMax, node.val).
Return Math.max(dfs(node.left, curMin, curMax), dfs(node.right, curMin, curMax)).

whyNext: Builds on bottom-up subtree postorder traversal from Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (Seq 134) by calculating the coin balance (coins - 1) of each subtree and accumulating abs(balance) moves.
hints: Each node requires exactly 1 coin. A subtree with N nodes and C coins has a net balance of C - N.
The net balance of coins must cross the edge connecting this subtree to its parent, requiring abs(balance) moves.
Postorder DFS: balance = node.val - 1 + leftBalance + rightBalance. Accumulate ans += abs(leftBalance) + abs(rightBalance). Return balance.

brute.idea: Iteratively simulate moving surplus coins to nearest deficit nodes using BFS tree distance calculation.
steps: Identify nodes with surplus coins (> 1) and deficit nodes (0 coins).
For each surplus coin, find closest deficit node via BFS.
Add distance to total moves and update coin counts.
Repeat until all nodes have exactly 1 coin.
brute.whySlow: Simulating individual coin moves across graph edges takes O(n^2) time.

optimal.idea: Bottom-up postorder balance aggregation: each edge transfers abs(subtree_balance) coins, running in O(n) time.
steps: Define dfs(node): if node == null return 0.
Compute leftBalance = dfs(node.left) and rightBalance = dfs(node.right).
Accumulate total moves += Math.abs(leftBalance) + Math.abs(rightBalance).
Return node.val - 1 + leftBalance + rightBalance.

whyNext: Builds on postorder state classification from Distribute Coins in Binary Tree (Seq 403) by returning 3 coverage states (0: uncovered, 1: covered without camera, 2: has camera) to greedily place cameras at parents of uncovered leaves.
hints: Place cameras from bottom to top: placing a camera at a leaf's parent covers the leaf, the parent, and the grandparent, which is always more optimal than placing it at a leaf.
Define 3 states: 0 = node is not covered, 1 = node is covered, 2 = node has a camera.

If either child is uncovered (0), current node must have a camera (2). If either child has a camera (2), current node is covered (1). Otherwise current node is uncovered (0). If root ends as 0, add 1 camera.

brute.idea: Tree DP computing min cameras for each node under 3 states: (has camera, covered by child, covered by parent).
steps: For each node, compute dynamic programming tuple (withCamera, coveredNoCamera, uncovered).
Combine states from left and right subtrees.
At root, return min(withCamera, coveredNoCamera).
brute.whySlow: State transitions in full tree DP require computing multiple branch configurations.

optimal.idea: Greedy postorder 3-state reduction: place cameras strictly at parents of uncovered nodes, minimizing camera count in O(n) time.
steps: State 0 = uncovered, State 1 = covered (no camera), State 2 = has camera.
In dfs(node): if null return 1.
Compute left = dfs(node.left) and right = dfs(node.right).
If left == 0 || right == 0: cameras++, return 2.
If left == 2 || right == 2: return 1.
Return 0.
If dfs(root) == 0, add 1 camera to cover root. Return cameras.

whyNext: Builds on tree serialization from Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (Seq 128) by hashing preorder subtree serialization strings and storing frequencies in a HashMap to collect roots with frequency exactly 2.
hints: Serialize each subtree as a string: node.val + "," + serialize(left) + "," + serialize(right).
Store serialized strings in a HashMap<String, Integer> to count occurrences.
When a serialized subtree string count reaches exactly 2, add the current node to the result list.

brute.idea: Serialize every subtree into a string and store in a map, comparing all subtree strings.
steps: Traverse tree postorder.
Generate serialized string for each subtree.
Update count in map.
If count == 2, add subtree root to result list.
brute.whySlow: String concatenation takes O(n) per node, resulting in O(n^2) overall time.

optimal.idea: Subtree ID mapping: assign unique integer IDs to (val, leftId, rightId) triplets to compress subtree serialization into O(n) time.
steps: Assign an integer ID to each unique (node.val, leftId, rightId) tuple using a HashMap.
Track frequency of each ID in a second map.
When an ID's frequency reaches 2, add the current node to result list.
Return assigned ID for the current subtree.

whyNext: Builds on column coordinate tracking from Binary Tree Right Side View (Seq 136) by sorting nodes first by column x, then by row y, then by node value for tie-breaking.
hints: Traverse tree tracking coordinates (row, col) for each node: root is (0, 0), left child is (row + 1, col - 1), right child is (row + 1, col + 1).
Nodes at the same column should be ordered by row; nodes with the same row and column must be sorted by their values.
Store triples (col, row, val) in a list, sort them using comparator (col, then row, then val), and group by col into sublists.

brute.idea: Traverse tree with DFS, collect all (col, row, val) tuples into a global list, sort them with custom comparator, and group by col.
steps: Traverse tree collecting (col, row, val) for each node.
Sort list by col ascending, then row ascending, then val ascending.
Group sorted tuples by col into List<List<Integer>>.
Return grouped list.
brute.whySlow: Sorting all n nodes together takes O(n log n) time.

optimal.idea: BFS coordinate traversal with TreeMap grouping: collect row buckets per column to sort only overlapping cell nodes in O(n log(n/k)) time.
steps: Use TreeMap<Integer, TreeMap<Integer, PriorityQueue<Integer>>>.
BFS queue stores (node, col, row).
Pop elements, add to map structure.
Iterate columns in TreeMap, then rows, then extract from min-heap.
Return grouped list of lists.

whyNext: Builds on in-order BST ordering from Validate Binary Search Tree (Seq 152) by comparing adjacent nodes in the sorted in-order traversal to minimize abs(current - previous).
hints: An in-order traversal of a Binary Search Tree produces values in strictly sorted ascending order.
The minimum difference between any two nodes must occur between two adjacent values in this sorted order.
Track prevNode during in-order traversal: minDiff = min(minDiff, node.val - prevNode.val); prevNode = node.

brute.idea: Perform in-order traversal to store all node values in a list, then scan adjacent pairs to find the minimum difference.
steps: Traverse BST in-order and append each value to an ArrayList.
Loop i from 1 to list.size() - 1.
Update minDiff = min(minDiff, list.get(i) - list.get(i - 1)).
Return minDiff.
brute.whySlow: Requires O(n) auxiliary list storage for all node values.

optimal.idea: In-order traversal with a single previous node reference: compute differences on the fly in O(1) auxiliary space.
steps: Maintain Integer prev = null and minDiff = Integer.MAX_VALUE.
In in-order traversal: recurse left subtree.
If prev != null: minDiff = Math.min(minDiff, node.val - prev).
prev = node.val.
Recurse right subtree. Return minDiff.

whyNext: Builds on complement lookup from Two Sum (Seq 2) by checking if k - node.val exists in a HashSet during tree traversal, or using two BST iterators for O(1) space.
hints: Use a HashSet to store visited node values. For each node, check if set.contains(k - node.val).
Alternatively, since it is a BST, an in-order traversal gives a sorted array, where standard two pointers can find the target sum in O(n) time.
In dfs(node, set, k): if node == null return false. If set.contains(k - node.val) return true. set.add(node.val). Return dfs(node.left) || dfs(node.right).

brute.idea: Perform in-order traversal to extract all elements into a sorted array, then use two pointers from both ends.
steps: Traverse tree in-order to build sorted ArrayList.
Set left = 0, right = list.size() - 1.
While left < right: sum = list[left] + list[right]. If sum == k return true; if sum < k left++; else right--.
Return false.
brute.whySlow: Requires extracting all elements into a separate list.

optimal.idea: One-pass HashSet traversal: check if complement k - node.val was seen, returning immediately upon match.
steps: Initialize HashSet<Integer> seen.
Define dfs(node): if null return false.
If seen.contains(k - node.val) return true.
seen.add(node.val).
Return dfs(node.left) || dfs(node.right).

whyNext: Reverses the in-order traversal from Minimum Absolute Difference in BST (Seq 407) by visiting right-root-left (reverse in-order) to accumulate a suffix sum of all greater node values.
hints: Every node needs its value increased by the sum of all nodes with values greater than it in the BST.
In a BST, all greater values lie in the right subtree.
Perform a reverse in-order traversal: recurse right, add current node's value to running sum, update current node's value with running sum, and recurse left.

brute.idea: For every node, traverse entire BST to sum all node values greater than it.
steps: For each node u in tree, compute sum of all v in tree where v.val > u.val.
Add this sum to u.val.
Return tree.
brute.whySlow: Traversing the entire tree for every node takes O(n^2) time.

optimal.idea: Reverse in-order traversal (right -> root -> left): accumulate suffix sum in a single pass in O(n) time.
steps: Maintain int runningSum = 0.
In reverseInorder(node): if null return.
reverseInorder(node.right).
runningSum += node.val; node.val = runningSum.
reverseInorder(node.left).
Return root.

whyNext: Builds on BST deletion mechanics from Delete Node in a BST (Seq 151) by discarding subtrees outside [low, high] and reconnecting the trimmed valid children in O(n) time.
hints: If node.val < low, all nodes in its left subtree are also < low, so the entire left subtree and node can be discarded; return trimBST(node.right, low, high).
If node.val > high, all nodes in its right subtree are also > high, so discard right subtree and node; return trimBST(node.left, low, high).
If low <= node.val <= high, keep node and trim both subtrees: node.left = trimBST(node.left, low, high) and node.right = trimBST(node.right, low, high). Return node.

brute.idea: Collect all BST values within [low, high] via in-order traversal and rebuild a balanced BST from the filtered list.
steps: Traverse tree and collect nodes satisfying low <= val <= high.
Sort or keep sorted list.
Reconstruct BST recursively using middle elements.
Return new tree root.
brute.whySlow: Allocates a new tree structure rather than pruning existing pointer links in place.

optimal.idea: Recursive in-place trimming: prune entire out-of-bounds branches by returning the valid child directly.
steps: If root == null, return null.
If root.val < low, return trimBST(root.right, low, high).
If root.val > high, return trimBST(root.left, low, high).
root.left = trimBST(root.left, low, high); root.right = trimBST(root.right, low, high).
Return root.

whyNext: Builds on sorted array to balanced BST conversion from Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree (Seq 154) by performing an in-order traversal to collect sorted node values and recursively bisecting the list to rebuild an optimally balanced BST.
hints: In-order traversal of an unbalanced BST produces all values in strictly sorted ascending order.
Given a sorted list of values, picking the middle element as root and recursing on the left and right halves builds a height-balanced BST.

Step 1: list = inorder(root). Step 2: build(list, left, right) creates node with val = list[mid], node.left = build(list, left, mid - 1), node.right = build(list, mid + 1, right). Return build(list, 0, list.size() - 1).

brute.idea: Rotate unbalanced nodes using AVL / Day-Stout-Warren vine tree rotations.
steps: Flatten tree into a right-skewed vine list via right rotations.
Count total nodes n.
Perform successive left rotations to rebalance into a complete binary tree.
Return root.
brute.whySlow: Pointer rotation rebalancing involves complex multi-phase pointer rewiring.

optimal.idea: In-order extraction followed by divide-and-conquer bisection: creates an AVL-balanced BST in O(n) time.
steps: Perform in-order traversal to populate sorted ArrayList<Integer>.
Recursively construct balanced BST by choosing mid = (l + r) / 2 as current node.
Recurse left subtree with [l, mid - 1] and right subtree with [mid + 1, r].
Return root.

whyNext: Builds on preorder tree reconstruction from Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal (Seq 140) by utilizing BST upper bound constraints to reconstruct the tree in a single pass without needing explicit inorder traversal.
hints: In preorder traversal, the first element is the root. All subsequent elements smaller than root belong to the left subtree, and elements greater belong to the right subtree.
You can reconstruct the BST by passing an upper bound parameter (bound) down recursive calls.

Maintain a global index pointer: if index == preorder.length or preorder[index] > bound, return null. Create node = new TreeNode(preorder[index++]); node.left = bstFromPreorder(node.val); node.right = bstFromPreorder(bound); return node.

brute.idea: For each node, find the boundary between values smaller than root (left subtree) and larger than root (right subtree), then recurse.
steps: First element is root.
Scan remaining elements to find index of first element greater than root.
Left subarray belongs to left subtree; right subarray belongs to right subtree.
Recurse on left and right subarrays.
brute.whySlow: Scanning for the split point on skewed trees takes O(n^2) time.

optimal.idea: One-pass upper-bound recursion: advance a global index pointer through preorder array, placing nodes according to BST upper bound in O(n) time.
steps: Maintain int idx = 0.
In bst(preorder, bound): if idx == preorder.length or preorder[idx] > bound, return null.
TreeNode root = new TreeNode(preorder[idx++]).
root.left = bst(preorder, root.val).
root.right = bst(preorder, bound).
Return root.
